A frescoed hall comes with one rule that is not negotiable: nothing touches the walls.

Which sounds simple until you put fifty covers in a room whose perimeter is out of bounds. The table goes down the centre, the service line runs behind the chairs, and the field kitchen goes two rooms away.

Ninety-one rooms in this dossier. Number six.

Syntonia — a travelling kitchen based in Florence. Private venues that are not venues, in Florence and across Tuscany.

Dessert in a glass is not laziness. It is arithmetic.

Fifty plated desserts take twenty minutes to assemble and six minutes to serve, which does not work. In a glass they are made in the morning, they sit in the fridge, and they come out together. By that hour the kitchen is already half dismantled, and this is the only way to do it without anybody noticing.

The spoon is long. That part is not an aesthetic choice.

Syntonia — a travelling kitchen based in Florence. Seasonal Tuscan cooking, plated where there is no kitchen.

The same hall, and nothing is touching the walls.

Fifty covers down the centre, the service line behind the chairs, the field kitchen two rooms away. That is the entire plan, and it is dictated by the frescoes rather than by us. No chandelier is switched on: the flames sit lower than the paintings, so the room reads and the ceiling goes dark.

Houses like this say yes to about one evening a season.

Ninety-one rooms in this dossier. Number six, at night.

Syntonia — a travelling kitchen based in Florence. We open rooms that are not for hire, for one evening, and put them back as we found them.

New oil is judged in the throat, not on the tongue.

The catch that arrives two seconds later is polyphenol, and if it is not there the oil is either old or it has been heated. It does not last: by March that oil is a different oil.

You buy it in November and you do not wait.

Syntonia — a travelling kitchen based in Florence. Seasonal Tuscan produce, cooked where the guests are.

At anchor there is no second run.

Whatever was forgotten stays forgotten, so the list is checked twice on the quay and once more before the lines come off. Water is the limit rather than power: a boat carries what it carries, and the washing up is done ashore the next morning.

Ninety-one rooms in this dossier. Number seven.

An amaro is chosen by the hour, not by what was eaten.

Before midnight the ones with more herb and less sugar; after midnight the other way round. That is why there are six on the trolley and not twenty, and why none of the six is poured at the table.

By then the kitchen has already gone back out through the door it came in.

Syntonia — a travelling kitchen based in Florence. We stay until the room is empty and put it back the way we found it.

An oyster is served cold, not iced.

It rests on the ice, never in it: if meltwater gets into the shell it carries off the liquor, which is the part you are paying for. And it is opened to order, because an oyster opened half an hour early has already lost twice.

Six minutes from the bench to the table. Beyond that, the menu changes.

Syntonia — a travelling kitchen based in Florence. We buy short and cook the same day, in houses with no kitchen.

A refectory was designed for exactly this, and then stopped being used for it.

One long wall of fresco, a stone floor that takes anything, and acoustics built for a single voice reading aloud, which means fifty people talking sound like two hundred. Cloth on the table and something soft at both ends, or the room wins.

Ninety-one rooms in this dossier. Number eight.

The second hour is the one that decides the evening.

By then the food is doing less work than the room: how loud it is, how far apart people are sitting, whether the light has come down. A table held at the same brightness from eight to midnight empties by eleven.

We take the light down twice. Nobody has ever mentioned it.

Syntonia — a travelling kitchen based in Florence. Long tables in Tuscan villas, cloisters and private houses.

The same refectory, and the problem is not the table. It is the echo.

A hall built so that a single voice would carry to the far end gives forty people back as two hundred. Fabric goes where it cannot be seen, under the cloth and at both ends, and the light comes down, because people speak more quietly in a darker room. It works, and nobody understands why.

By day the visitors walk through it. In the evening it belongs to whoever asked for it.

Ninety-one rooms in this dossier. Number eight, at night.

The door is the last thing we open.

Two hours before this the room was full of crates and four of us moving fast. By the time it opens there is nothing in here that belongs to us except the table, and the passage outside has been swept.

Nobody sees the two hours. That is the job.

Syntonia — a travelling kitchen based in Florence. We arrive with the brigade and the field kitchen, and leave the room as we found it.

At six in the morning Florence is a city of deliveries.

The trolley is on the paving because the van does not come in: inside the walls you unload at the gate and push, and the distance between the gate and the door decides how many times you go back and forth. Fifty covers is between four and six runs.

By seven the street belongs to the people who live on it again.

Syntonia — a travelling kitchen based in Florence. Private dinners in the city's houses, courtyards and top floors.

Dinner ends when somebody stands up, not when dessert is finished.

Which is why the next room has been ready for an hour: armchairs already grouped in fours, light two thirds lower than the dining room, and nothing to eat. Anyone who moves has to find a seat within three paces, or they go back to the table and the evening sits down again.

The move is never announced. A door is opened.

Syntonia — a travelling kitchen based in Florence. Private dinners in Tuscany, from the first glass to the swept floor.
